name: Carrow Thermal Henley
description:
A three-button henley cut from a dense cotton-polyester thermal weave, double-stitched at every stress point and pre-washed until the fabric has the soft, slightly pilled texture of something that's already survived a winter. Available in four colors: slate, rust, off-white, and a dark green that Carrow calls 'Fen.' The collar sits just high enough to layer under a jacket without bunching. The cuffs are ribbed and wide enough to accommodate most basic forearm augments without rolling up.

Carrow is a Tier 2 workhorse label out of what used to be Milwaukee's industrial west side — they make clothes for people who stand outside in November. The henley has been in their catalog for eleven years with almost no changes. That's the point. Dock workers, transit mechanics, warehouse supervisors, and anyone who needs a shirt that doesn't ask anything of them wear this. It just works.
what_it_says: You're practical, unpretentious, and you've been cold before. No performance, no statement — just someone who picks the right tool for the job and moves on.
story_hooks: A specific run of Carrow Thermal Henleys from 2197 was accidentally dyed with a batch of pigment that contains trace amounts of a restricted industrial solvent — long-term skin absorption is causing nerve numbness in some wearers, and Carrow is quietly trying to buy back the affected units before anyone files a claim.

A transit union organizer uses the Carrow Henley as an informal identifier — anyone showing up to a clandestine meeting wearing one is presumed sympathetic, a system that's worked until someone started wearing them who definitely isn't.
A character finds a Carrow Henley in a deceased relative's belongings, the cuffs still faintly stained with something they can't identify.
